opus-5.5.text:
I think, honestly, I was quite lucky. When I was finishing up and didn't really know what I wanted to do next, whether to stay in physics, do a postdoc, or jump into AI, nobody pressured me to make a decision quickly. The general attitude was very open: "You're young, you should explore. If something else excites you more, go try it."

That surprised me a bit at first. Coming from a more traditional academic path, I half expected people to say, "You've invested so many years in theoretical physics, why would you leave?" But in the Bay Area, people have seen so many students move between fields, into startups, into industry labs, and then sometimes back to academia. Changing direction isn't seen as a failure. It's seen as just another trajectory.

What I appreciated most was that the advice was very honest. People would tell me what they thought the trade-offs were, like what you might gain by staying in academia, what you might lose, and how fast things were moving in AI. But in the end they always said it's your call. That kind of respect for a student's own judgment gave me a lot of freedom, and also, I think, a bit more courage to take the risk.

So looking back, I feel grateful. The uncertainty was mine, but the environment made it much easier to sit with that uncertainty instead of panicking about it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says professors gave him time and freedom to explore while uncertain, but does not say they advised him to keep his current job during that uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I was pretty touched by how they handled it. When I was interviewing, I was very upfront that I wasn't sure what I wanted to do — whether I'd go to a lab like OpenAI, or stay in academia, or do something in between. That's not what you're supposed to say in a faculty interview. You're supposed to show up with a five-year research vision and a clear commitment.

But the professors I talked to at Berkeley, and at Stanford too, didn't really treat that as a red flag. A lot of them had been through the same thing themselves. Some had spent years at Google or OpenAI, some had gone back and forth. So the conversations weren't "convince us you'll stay," they were more like "okay, what are you actually trying to figure out, and what would help you figure it out?" That was a different kind of conversation from what I expected.

I think part of it is that the field is in a strange moment. The best work on language agents was happening in industry, and everyone knew it. A professor who pretended otherwise would have been a little dishonest. So they were realistic with me — they said, if you want to train frontier models, you can't really do that here, and you should know that. But they also pushed back on the idea that academia had nothing to offer. The argument was that in a lab you become a piece of a big machine, and in a university you get to define the problem yourself, even if you have less compute.

What I appreciated most was that nobody tried to rush me. A couple of people basically said, take the time, go to industry if that's what you need to do, and the door will still be open. Whether that's literally true, I don't know. But it changed how I thought about the decision. It stopped feeling like a one-way door and started feeling more like a question of sequencing — what do I need to learn first, and where can I learn it.

So I'd say they treated my uncertainty as a reasonable response to a genuinely confusing time, rather than as immaturity. I was grateful for that, and I try to remember it when I talk to students now who are facing the same thing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says professors treated the uncertainty as reasonable and advised taking time, including going to industry if needed. It does not attribute to them a view that someone should retain their current job while plans remain unsettled.

astra-6.text: I appreciated that they were willing to talk with me even though I hadn’t made up my mind. When you’re uncertain about your plans, it helps to have room to explore rather than feel you have to give a definite answer immediately. That openness was something I valued.

r001.rationale: The response says the professors gave him room to explore without deciding immediately, but it does not say they advised him to retain his current job while his plans were unsettled.

sol-6.1.text: What I appreciated was their willingness to give me room to figure things out. When your plans are uncertain, it helps to have people who take that uncertainty seriously without pushing you toward a particular answer. That’s the kind of support I value: helping you think through the decision while leaving it to you.

r001.rationale: The response describes professors giving room to think without pushing toward an answer, but does not say they advised keeping the current job while future plans were unsettled.
